cards.title: What Is OpenTelemetry?
cards.teaser: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus into a single, vendor-neutral framework for producing, collecting, and exporting telemetry. It is now the industry standard for instrumenting cloud-native software.

runs.text: Before 2019, the observability landscape was fragmented. OpenTracing defined a vendor-neutral tracing API. OpenCensus provided both a tracing and metrics API plus a collection agent. Both gained traction but split the community: library authors had to choose one, and operators had to run two agents. In May 2019, the two projects merged to form
OpenTelemetry
OpenTelemetry is governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and is today one of the highest-velocity CNCF projects. It provides:

items.text: — the normative definition of the API contracts, data models, and SDK behaviors.
— implementations in Go, Java, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, .NET, Ruby, PHP, Rust, C++, Erlang/Elixir, and more.
— a standalone binary that receives, processes, and exports telemetry to any backend.
— the OpenTelemetry Protocol, a vendor-neutral wire format for transmitting telemetry.

runs.text: The strategic promise of OTel is
instrument once, export anywhere
. A service instrumented with OTel can send its telemetry to Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana, Jaeger, or a custom backend by changing configuration, not code.

Major adopters include AWS (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry — ADOT), Google Cloud (native OTLP ingest in Cloud Trace and Cloud Monitoring), Datadog (OTel ingest via OTLP endpoint), Honeycomb, Grafana, and Dynatrace. Most observability vendors now accept OTLP natively.
OpenTelemetry is the one open standard for observability instrumentation — traces, metrics, and logs — so you write the instrumentation once and can send it to any tool without rewriting your code.

cards.title: The OTel Specification
cards.teaser: The OTel specification is the normative contract that all language SDKs must satisfy — it defines the API surface, the SDK behaviors, the data model, and the protocol. It is the source of truth, not any single SDK.

runs.text: OpenTelemetry separates concerns into three distinct layers, each covered by the specification:

items.text: — the minimal surface that application code and libraries use to record telemetry. The API is designed to be a no-op by default: if no SDK is configured, API calls do nothing and add negligible overhead. This means library authors can instrument against the OTel API without forcing their users to pull in a full SDK.
— the full implementation of the API. The SDK handles sampling decisions, batching, retry logic, and exporting. Applications configure the SDK at startup; libraries see only the API.
— the wire format specification for transmitting traces, metrics, and logs between the SDK, the Collector, and backends.

runs.text: The specification also defines semantic conventions (standardized attribute names), the resource model (metadata about the telemetry source), the context propagation mechanism (how trace context crosses process boundaries), and the data models for each signal type.
Signal maturity in the specification is tracked as:
Stable
(traces and metrics),
Stable
(logs as of OTel 1.x), and
Experimental
(profiles, still in progress). Language SDK maturity levels are tracked separately at opentelemetry.io/status.

The API/SDK split is what makes OTel safe to use in open-source libraries. A library that depends only on the OTel API adds essentially zero overhead to users who have not configured the SDK — and delivers full telemetry to users who have.

The OTel specification defines a thin API for recording telemetry (safe for libraries), a full SDK that does the real work (configured by applications), and a protocol for sending data to backends. The spec is the contract all language implementations must honor.

cards.title: OTel Signals: Traces, Metrics, and Logs
cards.teaser: OpenTelemetry treats traces, metrics, and logs as first-class signal types — each with its own data model, SDK instrumentation path, and OTLP wire representation. Understanding all three and their relationships is the foundation of effective observability.

runs.text: OTel defines three signal types, each serving a different observability purpose:

items.text: — a directed acyclic graph of spans representing the journey of a single request through a distributed system. Each span has a start time, duration, status, and attributes. Spans from different services are linked by a shared trace ID propagated in request headers (W3C TraceContext or B3).

— numeric measurements aggregated over time. OTel supports counters (monotonically increasing values, e.g., request count), gauges (instantaneous values, e.g., memory usage), and histograms (distribution of values, e.g., latency percentiles). The OTel metric data model is richer than Prometheus — it encodes temporality (cumulative vs delta) and exemplars (trace IDs linked to histogram buckets).

— structured or unstructured timestamped records. OTel's log data model attaches trace context (trace ID, span ID) to log records when available, enabling log-to-trace correlation without manual string interpolation.

runs.text: The three signals are correlated through shared
context

: a trace ID that appears in a span also appears in logs emitted during that span and in metric exemplars recorded at that time. This is what turns three separate streams of data into a coherent picture of system behavior.

OTel is also adding a fourth signal: profiling (continuous profiling). The profiling specification is in experimental status as of 2024 and aims to correlate CPU and memory profiles with trace spans for deep performance analysis.

OTel gives you traces (the story of one request), metrics (numbers over time), and logs (timestamped events). All three share a trace ID so you can jump between them — that linkage is what makes observability more than just three separate dashboards.

cards.title: Language SDKs
cards.teaser: OTel provides per-language SDK implementations that translate the vendor-neutral specification into idiomatic code for Go, Java, Python, JavaScript, .NET, Ruby, and more — each with stable and experimental components tracked separately.

runs.text: The OTel specification is implemented as language-specific SDKs. As of 2024, the following SDKs have reached stable status for traces and metrics:

items.text: — the reference implementation for many specification decisions; widely used in infrastructure tooling and Kubernetes-native workloads.
— includes a robust auto-instrumentation agent (a Java agent JAR) that instruments popular frameworks (Spring, gRPC, JDBC, Hibernate, Kafka) without source changes.
— instrumentation for Django, Flask, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Redis, Requests, and more. The auto-instrumentation entry point is
— both Node.js and browser environments are supported. Node.js auto-instrumentation patches require(), Express, HTTP, gRPC, and others.
Activity API so that existing .NET tracing code can emit OTel without rewriting.
— instrumentation for Rails, Rack, Sidekiq, ActiveRecord, Faraday.

runs.text: Each SDK ships as two packages: the
API package
(for libraries) and the
SDK package

(for applications). Libraries depend only on the API package. Application code configures the SDK — setting up exporters, resource attributes, and sampling — at startup, typically in a dedicated initialization block.

SDK maturity varies by language and by signal. Always check opentelemetry.io/status before assuming a signal is stable in your target language. A Go SDK that is stable for traces may still have experimental metrics instrumentation.

Each language gets its own OTel SDK that implements the spec idiomatically. Libraries take only the thin API package. Application code takes the full SDK and configures where telemetry goes — the library never needs to know.

cards.title: Auto-Instrumentation
cards.teaser: Auto-instrumentation agents inject OTel spans and metrics into popular frameworks without any source code changes — they work by patching the runtime, intercepting HTTP calls, and wrapping database drivers automatically.

runs.text: Auto-instrumentation is the fastest path to observability. It works by intercepting code at the framework or runtime level rather than at the application level:

items.text: ) uses bytecode manipulation (via the Byte Buddy library) to inject instrumentation into Spring MVC, Tomcat, gRPC, JDBC, Kafka, and dozens of other frameworks at class-load time. No recompilation needed.
CLI wraps your application process. It patches Django, Flask, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Redis, and HTTP clients using Python's monkey-patching mechanism. Equivalent to running:
flag patches require() at startup to wrap Express, HTTP, gRPC, databases, and message queue clients.
— the OpenTelemetry .NET Automatic Instrumentation uses CLR profiling APIs to instrument applications at runtime, similar to commercial APM agents.

runs.text: Auto-instrumentation covers the
framework layer
: inbound HTTP requests, outbound HTTP calls, database queries, gRPC calls, and message queue operations. It does
not

cover business logic inside your application. A span for "HTTP POST /checkout" tells you the endpoint was called; it does not tell you whether the inventory check or the payment processing sub-step was the bottleneck. For that, you need manual instrumentation.

AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) ships pre-configured auto-instrumentation for Lambda, ECS, and EC2 workloads. Enabling it requires only attaching a Lambda layer or a sidecar container — no code changes. This is the OTel model operating at cloud-provider scale.

Auto-instrumentation wraps your frameworks so spans and metrics appear with zero code changes. It covers the edges of your service — incoming requests, outgoing calls, database queries — but not the business logic inside, which needs manual instrumentation.

cards.title: Manual Instrumentation
cards.teaser: Manual instrumentation is the act of explicitly creating spans, recording attributes, and reporting metrics inside application code — it is how you make business logic observable, not just framework traffic.

runs.text: The following Python example shows the core manual instrumentation pattern: getting a tracer, creating a span, recording attributes, and handling errors.

explanation.text:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.trace import StatusCode

# Get a tracer scoped to this module
tracer = trace.get_tracer(__name__)

def process_order(order_id: str, user_id: str) -> dict:
    # Start a span for this business operation
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("process_order") as span:
        # Record structured attributes
        span.set_attribute("order.id", order_id)
        span.set_attribute("user.id", user_id)

        try:
            inventory = check_inventory(order_id)
            span.set_attribute("inventory.available", inventory["available"])

            result = charge_payment(order_id, user_id)
            span.set_attribute("payment.status", result["status"])
            return result

        except PaymentDeclinedError as e:
            # Record the error on the span
            span.set_status(StatusCode.ERROR, str(e))
            span.record_exception(e)
            raise

runs.text: Key patterns shown:

items.text: — scopes the tracer to the module. The tracer name appears in telemetry and helps locate the instrumentation source.
— creates a child span of whatever is currently active (the HTTP handler span from auto-instrumentation, for instance), maintaining the trace hierarchy automatically.
— attaches business context to the span. These attributes are searchable and filterable in any OTel-compatible backend.
— records the exception type, message, and stack trace as span events, following the OTel exception semantic convention.

runs.text: The same pattern in Go uses tracer.Start(ctx, "process_order") which returns a context and span. The child context is passed to downstream calls so the trace hierarchy propagates automatically through the call graph.

Manual instrumentation means explicitly wrapping business logic in spans and tagging them with meaningful attributes. You get a tracer, start a span with a name, set attributes that describe the operation, mark errors if they happen, and end the span when done.

cards.title: Resource Attributes
cards.teaser: Resource attributes are key-value metadata that describe the entity producing telemetry — the service name, version, host, cloud region, and Kubernetes pod. They appear on every span, metric, and log record emitted by a process.

runs.text: A
Resource

in OTel is the description of the entity that produced the telemetry. Unlike span attributes (which describe a single operation) or metric attributes (which describe a single measurement), resource attributes describe the
process itself
and are attached to all telemetry emitted by that process.
Common resource attributes defined by the OTel semantic conventions:

items.text: — the logical name of the service (e.g., "payment-service"). Required. Without it, backends cannot group telemetry by service.
— the deployed version (e.g., "1.4.2"). Enables correlation between deployments and error rate changes.
— unique identifier for this running instance (e.g., a UUID or pod name). Enables per-instance debugging.
— Kubernetes context, populated automatically by the OTel Kubernetes Attributes Processor or via the Downward API.
— cloud metadata, used to correlate cross-region latency.
— staging, production, canary. Separates traffic in multi-environment setups.

runs.text: Resource attributes are set once at SDK initialization, either via environment variables (
OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=service.name=payment-service,service.version=1.4.2
) or programmatically. Many backends use resource attributes as primary indexing dimensions, so setting them correctly is not optional — it is the prerequisite for useful dashboards and alerts.

Missing service.name is the single most common OTel configuration error. Backends group telemetry by service.name. Without it, all telemetry from a process lands in a bucket labeled "unknown_service" and becomes nearly impossible to query.

Resource attributes are the address label on every telemetry envelope — they tell backends what service, version, host, and environment produced the data. Set them once at startup and they appear on every span, metric, and log your process emits.

cards.title: Semantic Conventions
cards.teaser: Semantic conventions are the OTel specification's standardized attribute names — http.method, db.system, rpc.service, messaging.destination — that make telemetry queryable and comparable across services, languages, and teams.

runs.text: Without semantic conventions, every team invents its own attribute names. One service tags the HTTP method as
http_method
, another as
method
, a third as
verb
. The result is a telemetry corpus that cannot be queried uniformly. Semantic conventions solve this by defining the canonical attribute name for every common category of operation.
Key semantic convention namespaces:
Auto-instrumentation libraries follow semantic conventions automatically. Manual instrumentation should too — use the constants from your SDK's
semconv
package rather than string literals, so your attributes remain correct when the conventions are updated.

Semantic conventions are versioned and evolve over time (e.g., http.method was renamed to http.request.method in the HTTP semconv v1.21 stabilization). Observability backends that support OTel handle the aliasing — but using SDK semconv constants insulates your code from the churn.

Semantic conventions are the shared vocabulary for attribute names — they define that an HTTP method is always http.request.method, not method or verb. Following them means any OTel-compatible tool can query your telemetry without custom configuration.

cards.title: The OTel Collector
cards.teaser: The OTel Collector is a standalone binary that acts as a vendor-neutral telemetry pipeline: it receives telemetry from applications, processes it (filtering, batching, enrichment, sampling), and exports it to one or more backends.

runs.text: The Collector decouples application code from the observability backend. Instead of configuring each service with backend-specific credentials and endpoints, services send telemetry to the Collector over OTLP, and the Collector handles routing.
The Collector is structured as a pipeline of three component types:

items.text: — accept telemetry from sources. Built-in receivers include
, and cloud-specific receivers (AWS CloudWatch, GCP, Azure).
processor adds, removes, or renames attributes. The
processor makes sampling decisions after seeing a full trace.
exporter forwards to any OTLP-compatible backend. Others include

runs.text: A minimal Collector configuration sending spans to Jaeger and metrics to Prometheus:

explanation.text:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 1s
    send_batch_size: 1024
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512

exporters:
  jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger:14250
    tls:
      insecure: true
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:8889

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [jaeger]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [prometheus]

runs.text: The Collector has two distributions: opentelemetry-collector (core, maintained by the OTel project) and opentelemetry-collector-contrib (includes community components for Datadog, AWS, GCP, Kafka, and dozens more). Most production deployments use the contrib distribution.

The Collector is a telemetry router: it receives data from your services, optionally filters or enriches it, and sends it to wherever you want it to go. Changing backends means changing the Collector config, not touching your application.

cards.title: Exporters and Backend Pluggability
cards.teaser: OTel exporters are pluggable adapters that translate the internal telemetry representation into the format each backend expects — the pluggability is what makes "instrument once, export anywhere" a practical reality rather than a marketing promise.

runs.text: An exporter is the last component in the OTel pipeline. It translates the OTel internal data model into the wire format of a specific backend and handles transport (HTTP, gRPC, TCP).
Exporters exist at two levels:

items.text: — configured in the application SDK, export directly from the service to the backend. Simpler for small setups but couples the application to backend configuration.

— the application exports to the Collector over OTLP, and the Collector's exporter handles backend-specific translation. The preferred pattern for production: backend credentials never reach the application container.

runs.text: The most important exporters:

items.text: — forwards to any OTLP-compatible backend. Used to chain Collectors or send to Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, Google Cloud Trace, AWS X-Ray (ADOT), and the Datadog Agent (which accepts OTLP natively since agent v7.30).
— exposes OTel metrics as a Prometheus scrape endpoint. Essential for integrating OTel with Prometheus/Thanos/Mimir-based metric stacks.
— sends traces to Jaeger. Note: the Jaeger project now recommends using the OTLP receiver in Jaeger 1.35+ rather than the legacy Jaeger exporter.
— translates OTel trace and metric data into Datadog's format. Datadog now also accepts OTLP directly at its agent and backend, making the exporter optional.

runs.text: The trend is toward OTLP-first backends. Grafana Tempo, Honeycomb, Lightstep, and Google Cloud all accept OTLP natively. This means the OTLP exporter handles most cases — backend-specific exporters are increasingly a migration bridge rather than a permanent configuration.

An exporter is the adapter that takes OTel's internal format and speaks the language of a specific backend. Plug in a different exporter and your telemetry goes somewhere new — your instrumentation code does not change.

cards.title: Sampling Decisions
cards.teaser: Sampling is the mechanism for controlling what fraction of traces is recorded and exported. Getting it wrong means either drowning in data or missing the traces you need — and OTel gives you multiple places to make the decision.

runs.text: High-throughput services can generate millions of spans per minute. Recording all of them is expensive in storage and query cost. Sampling is the answer — but the decision of
where
and
how
to sample has significant consequences.
OTel provides two fundamental sampling locations:

items.text: — the sampling decision is made at the start of a trace, before any spans are recorded. The SDK's sampler (configured via
(sample 1-in-N traces deterministically by trace ID), and
(inherit the sampling decision from the parent span's context). Head sampling is low-cost but makes the decision blindly — you cannot preferentially keep slow or error traces.
— the sampling decision is deferred until the entire trace is assembled. The Collector's

processor applies policies: always keep traces with errors, keep traces with latency above a threshold, drop healthy fast traces. Tail sampling gives you much smarter retention but requires the Collector to buffer spans in memory until a trace is complete (typically 10-30 seconds).

runs.text: A production-recommended strategy: head-sample 100% in development and staging; use
traceidratiobased
at 5-20% in production, combined with tail sampling in the Collector to always retain error traces and slow outliers.

Sampling decisions must be consistent across all services in a trace. If service A samples in 10% of traces but service B samples independently, you will get orphaned spans — fragments of traces whose root was dropped by one service but kept by another. Use parentbased sampler so all services in a trace agree.

Sampling decides which traces to keep. Head sampling decides at the start (cheap but blind). Tail sampling decides after the trace completes (smart — can keep errors, drop healthy traffic). Both must be consistent across services or you get broken trace fragments.

cards.title: The OTLP Protocol
cards.teaser: OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol) is the vendor-neutral wire format for transmitting traces, metrics, and logs — it runs over gRPC or HTTP/JSON and is the lingua franca between OTel-instrumented services, the Collector, and OTLP-native backends.

runs.text: Before OTLP, every observability vendor had a proprietary agent protocol. Switching vendors meant replacing agents on every host and updating every service's configuration. OTLP changes this by defining a standard protocol that all parties speak.
OTLP has two transport options:

items.text: — uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. Default port: 4317. Preferred for high-throughput server-to-server communication within a cluster. Supports streaming and bidirectional flow control.

— uses HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 with either Protobuf or JSON encoding. Default port: 4318. Easier to use from browser environments and behind proxies that do not support gRPC. JSON encoding is useful for debugging (human-readable) at the cost of payload size.

runs.text: The OTLP data model is defined in the opentelemetry-proto repository as Protocol Buffer schemas. Key message types:

items.text: — contains ResourceSpans, which group spans by resource (service instance).
— contains ResourceMetrics, with scope and metric data points (gauge, sum, histogram, exponential histogram, summary).
— contains ResourceLogs, with log records that include trace context fields (trace_id, span_id, trace_flags).

runs.text: The SDK default OTLP endpoint is
http://localhost:4318
(HTTP) and
http://localhost:4317
(gRPC). Override with
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
environment variable. In a Kubernetes sidecar model, this points to the Collector sidecar; in a DaemonSet model, it points to the node-local Collector.

AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana, Dynatrace, and New Relic all accept OTLP natively as of 2024. The default SDK exporter is OTLP — meaning a freshly instrumented service already speaks the right protocol for virtually every major backend.

OTLP is the common wire format — the shipping container standard for telemetry. Services speak OTLP to the Collector; the Collector speaks OTLP to backends that support it natively. gRPC for efficiency inside a cluster, HTTP for everything else.

cards.title: The OTel Migration: Moving Off Vendor SDKs
cards.teaser: Migrating from a proprietary vendor SDK to OpenTelemetry is the most common large-scale observability project teams undertake today — it decouples engineering from vendor contracts and makes multi-backend or vendor-switch scenarios operationally feasible.

runs.text: Most organizations that adopted distributed tracing before 2020 did so with a vendor-specific SDK: Datadog's ddtrace, Jaeger's opentracing-go client, Zipkin's Brave, New Relic's agent, or Dynatrace's OneAgent. Each created a hidden coupling: the instrumentation code, the sampling decisions, and the data routing were all tied to a single vendor's assumptions.
The strategic case for migrating to OTel:

items.text: Changing observability backends no longer requires touching application code. The Collector configuration changes; the instrumentation does not. Datadog → Grafana Cloud becomes a Collector reconfiguration, not a rewrite.
Send the same trace data to a long-term archive (Grafana Tempo), a real-time backend (Honeycomb), and a security analytics platform simultaneously, from one Collector pipeline.
Open-source frameworks (Spring, Django, gRPC-Go, Rails) are instrumenting themselves with the OTel API. Adopting OTel means getting library telemetry for free as the ecosystem matures.

One OTel Collector per node replaces per-vendor agents. AWS ADOT, Datadog Agent, and New Relic Infrastructure agent can all be replaced or supplemented by the Collector, which fans out to each vendor's ingest endpoint.

runs.text: Migration patterns in practice:

items.text: — Datadog now accepts OTLP at the Datadog Agent (port 4317/4318) and at the Datadog backend directly. Teams can remove ddtrace, switch to the OTel SDK, and continue sending to Datadog via OTLP while they evaluate alternatives. No dashboard changes required.
— OTel ships OpenTracing compatibility shims in most SDKs. You can adopt the OTel SDK and keep legacy OpenTracing-instrumented libraries working without rewriting them.
— migrate one service at a time. The OTel Collector translates between old and new formats at the boundary, so instrumented and non-instrumented services coexist in the same trace.

runs.text: The OTel migration is not about saving money — it is about architectural optionality. Teams that have completed it report that subsequent decisions ("should we evaluate Honeycomb?", "can we add a second backend for our security team?") go from months-long projects to days-long Collector reconfigurations.

Migrating to OTel means your observability instrumentation is no longer tied to any vendor. Once done, switching backends or sending to multiple tools simultaneously is a configuration change, not an engineering project.
